The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

TORM (TRMD.A-DK): a very well-run product tanker owner is earning a windfall it does not control; the windfall is fading, and the model's total return to March 2028 is about -33%

14 November 2026. Share price DKK 238.6 (about USD 35.7) on 11 November 2026. Money in USD unless stated. Sources and conventions are in the end notes.

Terms: TCE (time charter equivalent) is freight revenue less voyage costs; TORM guides on TCE, and brokers' "revenue" forecasts are TCE. The "fleet rate" is the average TCE that TORM earns per ship per day. The "settled rate" is the fleet rate at which the market settles once the 2026 disruption ends. LR2, LR1 and MR are TORM's three product tanker classes, from largest to smallest. NAV is net asset value per share, with ships at brokers' valuations. "The model" is the Financial Analyst's model (update 2), and "the guideline multiple" is Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 8.86 times two-year-forward earnings.
#0

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one paragraphTORM is a very well-run shipping company earning a windfall it does not control. The investment case for the next 12 to 24 months turns on how that windfall ends and on what TORM earns afterwards. The case is about a fade in earnings: no lasting step-up in earnings power lies behind the windfall.
  1. One variable decides everything: the fleet rate. Each USD 1,000 per day of fleet rate is worth about USD 34m of EBITDA and USD 0.33 of EPS, and EPS is zero at a fleet rate of about USD 20,000 to 21,000 per day. The fleet rate rises from about USD 28,500 in FY2025 to about 53,700 in FY2026; the model then takes it to about 44,400 in FY2027 and to 26,000 to 27,000 from FY2028. EPS follows the fleet rate, from 11.23 in FY2026 to 2.09 in FY2028.
  1. Today's price buys two things: near-term dividends and a "stub". The dividends are about USD 9.6 a share, declared between now and March 2028 (27% of the price, of which about USD 3.7 is declared with the results on 3 March 2027). The stub is the remaining USD 26 or so, a claim on a nearly debt-free fleet that earns USD 1.6 to 2.1 a share at the model's mid-cycle rate.
  2. The value of the stub depends on one number: the settled rate. At the guideline multiple, today's price is fair only if the fleet rate settles near USD 30,000 per day, which is roughly what consensus assumes. The model assumes USD 26,000 to 27,000, and one-year charter rates imply less. Each USD 1,000 per day on the settled rate is worth about USD 2.8 a share, or 8% of the price.
  1. The model's total return is negative on both horizons: -32.7% to 31 March 2028 and -28.0% to 30 September 2029. My two asset-based cross-checks soften the return to between about -26% and -1%, and neither changes its sign.
  2. The skew is negative in size and in speed. The downside would arrive within weeks, while the upside accrues quarter by quarter. Even a year of extra disruption is worth only about USD 3 a share of extra dividend, because extra disruption postpones the fade without cancelling it. The window of favourable results and estimate revisions is about four months long and closes on 3 March 2027.
  3. The share price is ahead of the sell-side. FY2027 EPS estimates rose 21% in a month while the shares fell 19% in a week. Brokers have written the fade into their FY2027 estimates but kept a high floor under FY2028 that supports their price targets, and that FY2028 floor is the estimate most likely to be cut.
  4. TORM's strengths are real and durable, and they decide how TORM performs against its peers, not which way the shares go. The strengths are a commercial platform that earns about 10% more per day than peers, exact disclosure, a windfall that is permanently removing the debt, and a simplified shareholder structure with Hafnia as a 19.85% strategic holder.
  5. The constructive read: TORM fits none of Richard's Target Setups today, but it could fit one after the fade. A debt-free TORM with a proven rate premium, on the far side of the fade, could fit the setup "CfC in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough". The practical task now is to track the signposts and their trigger levels, which are public and mostly weekly (#9).

What works for the shares in the next 12 to 24 months

  • A record Q4 2026 dividend of about USD 3.7, declared on 3 March 2027, with FY2026 guidance close to locked.
  • Debt retired by the windfall stays retired: net debt falls from USD 840m at the end of 2025 to about USD 0.1bn by 2028.
  • Hafnia's 19.85% stake is an undated option on a combination near NAV.
  • Persistent disruption (20% likely) would extend the windfall and add about USD 3 a share of dividends.

What works against the shares

  • The leading indicators (crude tanker rates, freight futures, Brent) turned together in the week to 13 November.
  • An order book of about 20% of the fleet delivers mostly in 2028 and later, into the fade.
  • The FY2028 consensus median is 60% likely to be cut by more than 10% by May 2028.
  • On the model's earnings the shares trade at 13.1 times, above the 90th percentile of their ten-year range.

J

The five judgements that move the value of the shares most, with the arithmetic

Judgement 1: when the fade starts (the FY2027 fleet rate)

The model assumes a FY2027 fleet rate of about USD 44,400 per day on about 34,000 earning days (TCE of USD 1,509m), falling through the year from 63,000 in Q1 to 48,000, 36,000 and 31,000 in Q2 to Q4.

  • If normalisation is already under way in Q1 2027 (a fleet rate of about USD 32,000): TCE falls by (44,400 - 32,000) × 34,000 days = USD 422m. Because costs are fixed, EBITDA falls by the same USD 422m, from 1,121m to about 700m. Depreciation (252m) and net financial items (45m) do not move, and tax is under 1%, so net income falls from 819m to about 400m. On 103.7m shares, EPS falls by 4.0, from 7.90 to about 3.9. At a 75% payout the dividend falls from 5.95 to about 2.9. Free cash flow falls from 1,024m to about 600m, and net debt at the end of 2027 is about USD 100m higher.
  • If disruption lasts through 2027 (a fleet rate of about USD 55,000): TCE rises by 10,600 × 34,000 = USD 360m, EPS rises by 3.5 to about 11.4, and the dividend rises to about 8.5.
  • Rule of thumb: each quarter by which the fade comes earlier or later moves TCE by (63,000 - 31,000) × 8,500 days = USD 272m, which is about USD 2.6 of EPS and USD 2.0 of dividend.
  • A sub-lever that needs no peace deal: LR2 and LR1 ships provide about 32% of earning days (about 10,900 in 2027), and the model assumes they average about USD 52,000. If LR2 ships returning from crude cargoes to product trades (#1) take that average to USD 40,000, TCE falls by 12,200 × 10,900 = USD 133m and EPS by about 1.3.

Judgement 2: where the rate settles (FY2028 to FY2030)

The model assumes a settled fleet rate of USD 27,000, 26,000 and 26,500 in FY2028 to FY2030, giving FY2028 EBITDA of USD 520m, net income of 219m, EPS of 2.09 and a dividend of 1.58. That settled rate is already about double the fleet rate TORM earned in 2018 and 2021, and above the whole pre-2022 range restated in today's costs.

  • If the settled rate is wrong by USD 3,000 per day in either direction (the level of about 24,000 implied by one-year charter rates on one side, the 29,300 implied by the consensus median on the other): TCE and EBITDA move by 3,000 × 34,000 = USD 102m, to 418m or 622m. Net income moves by 100m after 2% tax, to 119m or 319m. On 104.9m shares, EPS moves by 0.95, to about 1.14 or 3.04, which is 46% either way. The dividend moves to about 0.86 or 2.28.
  • In value: at the guideline multiple of 8.86 times, 0.95 of EPS is USD 8.4 a share, 24% of today's price.
  • The same arithmetic decodes the brokers: Pareto's FY2028 EPS of 3.68 implies a fleet rate of about USD 31,900, and Clarksons' 5.57 implies about USD 37,900.

Judgement 3: what the ships are worth once rates normalise, and which anchor the market then uses

Brokers value the fleet at USD 4,333m, 53% above its book value of 2,838m, which gives a NAV of USD 39.60 a share.

  • If ship values fall 25% (Jefferies' downside case, roughly a return to 2025 prices): 4,333m × 25% = USD 1,083m, or USD 10.5 a share on 102.8m shares. NAV falls to about 29 before retained cash, and to about 34 to 38 by 2028 after retained cash (an estimate from the second set of research).
  • Earnings and dividends do not change, because TORM pays dividends out of profit, and the book value of the fleet is not written down unless ship values fall by more than a third. Net interest-bearing debt rises from 16% of fleet value (697m over 4,333m) to 21% before the cash build.
  • In value: tanker shares have troughed at 0.6 to 0.7 times NAV, so each 10% on ship values (USD 433m, or USD 4.2 a share of NAV) is worth USD 2.5 to 3.0 of share price.

Judgement 4: whether the cost stack keeps rising faster than modelled

The model grows vessel operating cost per day by about 4% a year, from USD 8,000 in 2026 to 9,300 in 2030. TORM's record since 2021 is about 5% a year, and 2026 is running at 6% to 9%.

  • At 7% a year: FY2028 cost per day is 8,000 × 1.07² = 9,160 against the model's 8,700; 460 × about 34,900 ship-days = USD 16m, or 0.15 of EPS (7%). By FY2030 cost per day is 8,000 × 1.07⁴ = 10,490 against 9,300; 1,190 × about 35,600 ship-days = USD 42m, or 0.39 of EPS (24%).
  • A second item: the model needs about USD 23m a year of "other operating income" to reconcile TCE with EBITDA, and the research files do not identify its source. If that income did not recur, EPS would be about 0.21 lower in every year.
  • Together in FY2028: the two items cost USD 39m, or 0.36 of EPS (17%), and they raise the fleet rate at which EPS is zero by about USD 1,150 per day.

Judgement 5: what the board, or Hafnia, does with the surplus

The model assumes a 75% payout, no buybacks and no ship purchases beyond the existing renewal programme. On those assumptions net debt falls to about USD 0.1bn by the end of 2028 and turns to net cash by 2030.

  • A buyback of USD 150m at USD 25 a share retires 6.0m shares, 5.7% of the count, and lifts FY2028 EPS from 2.09 to about 2.22.
  • A payout of 90% lifts the FY2028 dividend from 1.58 to about 1.88.
  • A combination with Hafnia could remove USD 40m to 70m a year of overhead (an estimate from the second set of research). The saving is worth USD 0.4 to 0.7 per TORM share if TORM's holders kept all of it, and about half that in a merger at NAV.
  • The adverse version: a payout five points lower while the 2029 newbuilding instalments fall due would take about 7% off the dividend, and ships bought with new shares would dilute holders, as they did in 2023 to 2025.
#1

Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

The tailwinds are exceptional today but borrowed, correlated and already weakening at the leading edge, while the headwinds are dated and locked in, so the external picture is strong for about two quarters and adverse for the 12 to 24 month case.

Evidence. Four forces have stacked on top of one another in 2026, and all four create distance and dislocation, not extra cargo. The headwinds, by contrast, arrive on a known schedule.

The newest evidence, from 9 to 13 November, is that the leading indicators turned together:

Leading indicatorMoveStatus
Crude tanker rates-37% to -47% in a weekTurned
A transatlantic tanker rateHalved in five days, on a proposal to reopen the Strait of HormuzTurned
January freight futuresHalved since 2 NovemberTurned
Brent crudeDown more than 20% from its high, to about USD 92Turned
Oil stocks (International Energy Agency)A 52 million barrel build in OctoberTurned
Container lines in the Red SeaCapacity through the Red Sea doubledTurned
Product tanker rates (9 November)MR about USD 65,000 per day; LR2 about USD 297,000Not yet
The leading edge of the tanker market has already turned. Only product tanker rates, which are the rates TORM earns, have not yet followed.

Inference. Three of the four forces are reversible and linked, so the downside would arrive as a cluster. One of the four, the migration of LR2 ships into crude, does not need a peace deal to reverse. LR2 ships went into crude because crude paid more; on the latest weekly data an LR2 in product trades earns about USD 126,000 per day more than a crude ship of the same size. Switching back costs USD 0.75m to 1.0m and 25 to 30 days, and in 2021 and 2022 a gap of under USD 2,000 per day was enough to move ships.

If the current rate gap persists for a few weeks, the return of LR2 ships to product trades will have started, and the extra supply would reach TORM's LR2 earnings in Q1 and Q2 2027.

So what. The operating environment is the best TORM has known, but it is a rent on scarcity with only one to two quarters of visibility. The topic's test (strong or improving tailwinds and no headwinds) is met today and failed over the 12 to 24 month horizon that matters. The 2026 spike is a squeeze on how the fleet is deployed, and such squeezes reverse faster than they build.

Counter-case. Management calls the 2026 market a multi-year "structural reset", and Jefferies and Morgan Stanley argue that the cycle extends beyond 2027. They have precedent: the 2022 dislocation lasted three years and outran every forecast. One ceasefire has already collapsed this year. The physical unwinding is slow (mine clearance in the Strait alone takes 30 to 50 days). Product trades do not accept ships older than 15 years back from crude, which caps the LR2 return. And 22% of the product tanker fleet is 20 years old or more, so scrapping can absorb deliveries once rates fall.
What would change my view. The number of LR2 ships in product trades staying below about 180 into Q1 2027 despite the rate gap; MR spot rates holding above about USD 50,000 per day into January; a collapse of negotiations; and, for the outer years, demolitions returning toward the 81 ships of 2021 from about six a year.
Against the market. The sell-side's commentary says the fade will be slow. Investors fear it will be fast, and sold the whole group on one headline. I am close to investors on the direction. I differ from both on one point: the return of LR2 ships to product trades may already have been triggered by the rate gap, without any settlement, and neither commentary nor product tanker rates reflect that yet.
Score: 20set by the Rater. The 2026 windfall is a rent on scarcity (Hormuz shut, Red Sea halved, two-thirds of LR2s in crude, shadow fleet) that is reversible, correlated and already turning at the leading edge (crude rates -37% to -47% in a week, January futures halved), while the headwinds are dated and locked in (order book about 20% of fleet, 63% delivering from 2028), so external forces take TCE from about USD 1.84bn to about 0.92bn by FY2028; consensus sales growth at the 0.2nd percentile tells the truth. I depart from the group's 46 because over two to three years the forces remove about half of revenue, not a near-neutral amount; better than Maersk thanks to a smaller order book, an old fleet that can scrap and two near-locked quarters, so between BP and Imperial Brands.
#2

Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Internal change at TORM is genuine in ownership and governance and absent in operations, so it offers an event option and a stronger balance sheet but no earnings driver of its own.

Evidence. The change inside TORM is in who owns the company and how it is governed, not in how it operates.

  • Ownership and governance: Oaktree, the controlling owner for a decade, sold its last shares at about USD 40 in early October 2026. The second and third share classes were cancelled in January 2026. The chair is independent, a former investment banker, and leads a Transaction Committee. Free float is about 80%, and the shares enter the OMX Copenhagen 25 index on 1 December, which brings passive buying of about half a day's trading volume.
  • Hafnia: TORM's largest competitor holds about 19.85% at an average cost of about USD 25.3 a share, having paid USD 32.25 and 34.00 for its September purchases. Hafnia said in February 2026 that it wanted to explore a combination. It has since changed chief executive and raised USD 300m of equity, and it reports results on 18 November.
  • Operations: the operating model is deliberately unchanged. There is no margin programme, no new market and no financial target beyond the current year. Costs are drifting up (administration costs rose 19% in 2025). The payout has been trimmed to 73% to 75% of profit to fund a fleet renewal programme ordered at record shipyard prices: six MR resales for 2027 to 2028, eight MR newbuildings for 2029 to 2030 and a half share of eight LR2 newbuildings, with USD 609m committed before the LR2 joint venture.
  • Shareholder dissent: more than 20% of votes went against the pay report and the buyback authority in April 2026; a revised pay policy comes to the 2027 annual meeting.

Inference. None of the internal change raises earnings. Four years of governance repair moved TORM's price to NAV from about 0.88 to about 0.92 times the peer group's, a gain of four points.

The Hafnia option is real but narrower than it looks. A deal is most likely to be share-for-share near NAV, because Hafnia's shares trade at about 1.1 times NAV and TORM's at 0.9, and that currency advantage lasts only while the sector holds its rating. The research files also conflict on whether the UK Takeover Code protects TORM's minority holders: one passage cites TORM's prospectus supplement of 7 October 2026 as saying that the Code will not apply after 2 February 2027. If that passage is right, a holder could pass 30% from that date without making an offer to all shareholders, and until the point is checked the Hafnia option is partly a risk.

Check before taking a position: whether TORM's prospectus supplement of 7 October 2026 says the UK Takeover Code stops applying after 2 February 2027.

So what. TORM has no self-help to replace the external forces when they fade. The internal story changes three model inputs (the payout, the capital spending schedule and a share count growing about 1% a year) and adds one event option. Part of the windfall is being recommitted to ships that deliver into the supply wave of 2028 and later.

Counter-case. The most valuable internal change is the one nobody announces: the windfall is retiring TORM's debt for good. Net debt was USD 840m at the end of 2025, will be about 420m to 450m at the end of 2026 once the Q4 dividend is paid in March, and falls to about 0.1bn by 2028. A board with no controlling holder and a cash surplus could make TORM's first well-judged capital decision, a buyback below NAV. Renewal is also needed, since about half the LR2 fleet is approaching 20 years of age.
What would change my view. A buyback executed below NAV; charter cover taken on 2027 and 2028 days at today's term rates (one-year rates of about USD 37,000 to 43,000 per day for a modern MR); an offer from Hafnia with terms; or cost guidance that commits management to a number.
Against the market. Investors treat the Hafnia stake as a takeover option, and in my view the stake is part of why TORM trades above Scorpio on NAV. I value the stake lower, as an option on a merger at about NAV with uncertain minority protection. I agree with the market that the end of Oaktree's selling is a positive, and that the positive is small.
Score: 48set by the Rater. The internal change is in ownership and governance (Oaktree out, share classes cancelled, independent chair, index entry, a 19.85% Hafnia stake as an undated option that may also be a minority-protection risk) and none of it raises earnings, while the operating model is unchanged, administration cost rose 19%, the payout was trimmed to fund newbuilds ordered at record yard prices delivering into the supply wave, and more than 20% voted against pay. I sit below the group's 54 because the peak-price capital commitments and cost drift offset the governance gains within three years, so a shade below Hexatronic's real self-help and above Indus Holding.
#3

Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

TORM is a top-tier operator with sound finances inside a fragmented, price-taking industry, with an execution edge of about 10% on the rate and no structural moat, so its foundations are below average for a listed European company and adequate for a cyclical.

Evidence. TORM earns more per day than its peers but also needs more per day to break even.

  • Structure: the top five owners hold under 15% of capacity and TORM about 3% (95 ships: 64 MR, 22 LR2 and 9 LR1). Rates clear daily on the spot market, customers are transactional, and owners order ships at peaks; every listed peer, TORM included, is ordering now.
  • Advantage: TORM's integrated "One TORM" commercial platform earns a measurable premium: USD 32,600 per day on MRs since 2022, against a peer average of 29,800. The premium was under USD 1,500 per day in 2018 and 2021 and nil against the best peer in single quarters, so it behaves as about 10% of the rate rather than as a fixed sum.
  • Cost: TORM's cash breakeven is about USD 15,000 to 16,000 per day, against under 11,000 at Scorpio, about 11,000 at Ardmore and about 13,000 at Hafnia. TORM's fleet is about 11 years old, against about 10 for peers.
  • Financial profile: return on invested capital was 26% in Q3 2026 and in the low single digits in 2017 to 2021; tax is near zero; earnings are clean. Free cash flow after fleet spending was negative in 2023 to 2025, and the share count rose 26% from 2022 for 22% more ships, so fleet growth added nothing per share.
  • Management: the chief executive has run TORM for 16 years, bought ships well in 2017 to 2018, and discloses exactly what an analyst needs. He has not bought back shares even at 0.6 to 0.9 times NAV, he issued shares near highs, and he earned USD 9.3m in 2025 under a bonus scheme that pays near its maximum whenever the market is strong.

Inference. The operator is better than the business. TORM's rate premium and its breakeven gap to peers are about the same size with opposite signs, and in a trough the premium shrinks with the rate while the breakeven gap does not. TORM sets no stretching goals because it sets no goals beyond the current year. TORM is a competent, honest, rate-taking company, and it passes Viewforth's test for this topic (favourable structure, barriers to entry, above-average financials and dynamic management) only on disclosure and execution.

The operator is better than the business: in a trough the rate premium shrinks with the rate, while the breakeven gap to peers stays.

So what. TORM's foundations justify trading around NAV through the cycle, not above it, and they decide how TORM performs against peers, not where the group goes. For Richard's Target Setups TORM is a decent-quality cyclical; it is not a high-quality, low-cyclicality business.

Counter-case. The premium is evidenced across a full cycle (over USD 200m on MRs in 2023 to 2025), and at a fleet rate of USD 27,000 the premium would still be about 40% of FY2028 net income. Falling interest costs close about USD 1,000 per day of the breakeven gap by 2028. Full shipyards physically constrain new supply for three years.
What would change my view. The MR premium holding at USD 2,500 per day or more as rates fall through USD 30,000 (testable each quarter against Scorpio, Ardmore and Hafnia); the cash breakeven falling toward USD 13,000; and a first buyback.
Against the market. Brokers describe TORM as the premier pure play and a "cash machine", and the market pays 0.90 times NAV for TORM against 0.78 for Scorpio. I agree on execution. I do not think trough economics justify TORM's premium to Scorpio, which has USD 1.4bn of net cash and a breakeven USD 4,000 to 5,000 per day lower.
Score: 32set by the Rater. A fragmented, price-taking spot industry (top five under 15%, TORM 3%, owners ordering at peaks) with an operator premium of about 10% of the rate that is offset by a breakeven USD 2,000 to 5,000 per day above peers, competent and transparent management but weak capital allocation (no buybacks below NAV, issuance near highs, fleet growth adding nothing per share), and low predictability; the peak figures (EBITDA margin 83rd percentile, ROIC 9.2% at the 63rd, 26% in Q3) do not tell the truth against low single-digit ROIC in 2017-2021 and newbuilds bought at record prices. Coherent with the groups (30, 32, 50, 58), it sits just below Solid State and above Ithaca.
#4

Conservatism of guidance, management of expectations, and the track record

TORM's guidance is conservative and reliable for FY2026 only; its record of raising guidance is a record of rising rates, and neither the company nor the sell-side is keeping expectations for 2028 low.
4 raisesFY2026 TCE guidance midpoint from USD 1,050m in February to 1,825m in November
88%of 2026 days covered; 53% of Q4 days booked at USD 78,419
60,400 / 78,900 / 97,400open Q4 rate needed for the bottom, midpoint and top of the range

Evidence. FY2026 guidance is close to locked after four raises. The current TCE range is USD 1,750m to 1,900m and the EBITDA range USD 1,350m to 1,500m; the EBITDA range is simply the TCE range less a round USD 400m of cost.

TORM's first guidance of each year is the more important evidence, and that first guidance has followed the direction of rates:

TORM gives no guidance beyond the current year and has no mid-term financial targets. Only four brokers publish estimates, and only two publish FY2028 estimates.

Inference. TORM's guidance method is "what is booked, plus the open days at about 78% to 88% of the booked rate". That method is conservative when rates rise after the guidance and not when they fade, and FY2027 is expected to be a fading year. TORM's reputation as a serial upgrader therefore describes the market of 2025 and 2026, not a habit that can be extrapolated.

The same record makes TORM's first FY2027 range, due on 3 March 2027, a two-sided event. If Q1 is booked near USD 60,000 per day and TORM uses its usual method, the TCE midpoint would be USD 1,700m to 1,850m, well above the consensus of 1,466m. I expect a deeper discount this time, because one-year charter rates are far below spot rates and the board itself calls visibility "extremely limited". My probabilities for the midpoint are 45% for more than 5% below consensus, 25% for within 5%, and 30% for more than 5% above.

TORM also does not talk expectations down: the chief executive's public framing of the market runs above the formal numbers.

So what. The topic's three tests (conservative guidance, expectations kept low and a record of raising) are met for the next results and for no period after them. The single most useful number on 3 March 2027 is the open-day rate implied by the bottom and the midpoint of the FY2027 range, because that rate is management's first statement in figures of what the rest of 2027 is worth.

Counter-case. FY2026 EBITDA could still exceed the top of the range (about 15% likely), and an unscheduled raise before March is possible (about 20% to 25%) if LR2 rates hold. On the one usable precedent, 6 March 2025, a strong dividend outweighed cautious guidance, and March 2027 brings the largest dividend in TORM's history.
What would change my view. A FY2027 range whose bottom assumes open days at about USD 35,000 per day or less, combined with new charter cover. That combination would turn guidance back into a floor with room to rise.
Against the market. The prevailing description, in broker commentary and in our own earlier work, is "always meets or beats, conservative by method", with March guidance expected below consensus as a matter of method. I differ on both points: the record depends on the direction of rates, and the March range is open in both directions.
Score: 57set by the Rater. Guidance is specific and mechanically conservative for the current year (FY2026 raised four times, 88% of days booked), but the record is rate-dependent: the FY2023 range was cut and the FY2024 top cut before two years of beats as rates rose, there are no targets beyond the year, and management talks above its numbers rather than keeping expectations low, leaving the March 2027 first range two-sided. Between the group's guidance 62 and sell-side 28, it sits like Renew's cut-then-beat record, just below it and above CVS.
#5

Pricing power, operating and financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

TORM has extreme operating leverage and no pricing power, cost flexibility or reinforcing loop of its own, so the business model magnifies whatever the rate does, and over this horizon the rate is expected to fall.

Evidence.

  • Operating leverage is extreme. About USD 700m a year of cost, depreciation and interest is fixed, against TCE of USD 0.9bn to 1.8bn. From FY2025 to FY2026 TCE doubles and EPS rises 3.9 times. In reverse, from FY2026 to FY2028 TCE falls 50%, EBITDA 64% and EPS 81%.
  • The sensitivity of EPS rises as rates fall. A 10% error on the fleet rate is about 18% of FY2027 EPS and about 42% of FY2028 EPS.
  • The breakeven is drifting up. The fleet rate at which EPS is zero rises from about USD 19,300 per day in FY2025 to about 20,600 in FY2028. At FY2025's fleet rate, FY2028's cost base would give EPS of about 2.6, against the 2.9 that TORM earned in FY2025.
  • TORM has no pricing power over the market; its only company-specific price element is the rate premium (#3).
  • Financial leverage is small: each USD 100m of net debt costs about USD 0.06 a share.
  • Cost reduction is nil net of inflation; the only large cost lever is a combination with Hafnia (Judgement 5).
  • The feedback loops act in a known order (figure below). One loop is specific to TORM: its capital spending peaks in 2029 (USD 294m), the weakest year for rates.

Inference. The topic asks whether revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth. At TORM it does, in both directions, and revenue is about to shrink. The same gearing that made TORM the best performer in its group on the way up (the highest share of spot days, the highest breakeven and the most LR2 earnings in Q4 bookings) makes TORM the most exposed of its group on the way down.

So what. Over 12 to 24 months TORM's operating leverage is the risk, not the opportunity. The order of the feedback loops gives the shape of the base case: a fast first leg down in 2027, a cushion, a slower second leg as deliveries arrive, and a floor only when scrapping resumes.

One constructive point: debt repaid during a windfall does not come back when rates normalise, so equity holders will own a larger share of TORM's enterprise value at the next trough than at the last one (#11).
Counter-case. If disruption persists, the operating leverage pays again (Judgement 1), and the cushions are real: the working-capital release alone is worth about USD 1.8 a share in 2027.
What would change my view. TORM fixing part of its book on time charters. Covering 20% of 2027 days at about USD 45,000 per day would raise FY2027 EPS by about 0.9 in the early-normalisation case and lower it by about 0.7 if disruption persists, which would remove about a fifth of the range of outcomes.
Against the market. The market understands TORM's operating leverage. It under-recognises two things: the same fleet rate now earns less than it did in 2025, and the newbuilding payments land in the weakest year for rates. Both are unfavourable.
Score: 38set by the Rater. The structure has extreme operating leverage, with about USD 700m of fixed cost, depreciation and interest so EBITDA moves one-for-one with TCE (TCE x2 gave EPS x3.9; TCE -50% gives EPS -81%), but no pricing power beyond the 10% premium, no net cost-out, small financial leverage and loops that reinforce the fall over this horizon, so the gearing works against the company as revenue shrinks. Above Maersk's similar price-gearing case because TORM's cost base is more fixed and the balance sheet is de-gearing, but well below BP's 50.

#7

Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

There is scope for modest upgrades until 3 March 2027 and a greater likelihood of cuts thereafter, concentrated in FY2028, so the upgrade skew is positive only briefly and where it matters least.

Evidence and inference. The scope for upgrades is real, narrow and front-loaded.

  • To 3 March 2027 (favourable). The FY2026 consensus mean should rise about 4% when one broker, whose TCE estimate sits below the bottom of TORM's guidance range, catches up (75% likely). Q4 2026 will be the record quarter (EPS about 4.9) with the record dividend. The FY2027 consensus median is about as likely to rise as to fall over this window (up more than 5% at 40%, down more than 5% at 35%), depending on whether winter rates hold.
  • After March (unfavourable). Revision breadth (analysts raising less analysts cutting), at its maximum today, has about an even chance of turning negative within six months and a 70% chance within twelve. I put a cut of more than 10% to the FY2028 consensus median by May 2028 at 60%. Guidance through 2027 is equally likely to be raised, held or cut, against four raises in 2026, and TORM's first FY2028 guidance is 70% likely to sit below today's FY2028 consensus.
  • The dividend narrative has one more step up and then several steps down. The quarterly dividend runs about USD 3.7, 2.6, 1.7, 1.0 and 0.7 from Q4 2026 to Q4 2027 in the base case. For yield investors that sequence is the most visible signal still to come.
  • Precedent: estimate cuts follow the turn in rates; they do not anticipate it. After the Q1 2024 peak, brokers raised the current year and trimmed the next year in the same notes, and the large cuts came nine months later. Consensus EPS for FY2025 peaked at 5.30, and the outcome was 2.91.

The dates.

So what. The scope for upgrades lasts about four months and sits in FY2026 and FY2027, which carry little of the valuation. The scope for cuts sits in FY2028, which carries most of the valuation.
Counter-case. Winter rates hold, Q1 2027 is booked above USD 60,000 per day, the March range lands above consensus and negotiations fail: that combination would produce another leg of upgrades to FY2027 and push the peak out. The lag between spot and booked revenue could also produce small beats in the first falling quarters; I treat that as a hypothesis, because TORM's documented quarterly misses were caused by cost and finance lines.
What would change my view. A sequential rise in peers' Q1 bookings in February; brokers lifting FY2028 on evidence (scrapping, LR2 counts) rather than on spot rates; a first buyback.
Against the market. All four brokers rate the shares Buy, with a mean target about 30% above the price. I think their FY2028 numbers are the vulnerable ones. The share price already agrees with me more than with them.
Score: 21set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, has a small favourable window (FY2026 mean catching up about 4%, a record Q4) but the first FY2027 range in March is 45% likely to land more than 5% below consensus against 30% above, guidance through 2027 is as likely cut as raised, and the first FY2028 guide is 70% likely below consensus; the price-driving FY2028 median is 60% likely cut by more than 10%, and the narrative has one step up then several down. The assumptions the base case requires.

#10

Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The stock is at peak delivery, in late Reinforcing with the first signs of Stalling, one phase later than the dashboard's rule-based "Broadening".

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places TORM in "Broadening". The facts fit a later point in the lifecycle.

  • Signs of Reinforcing at peak delivery: four guidance raises, estimates still rising, a record quarter and a record dividend ahead, and unanimous Buy ratings.
  • First signs of Stalling: the shares fell on good news; the adjacent crude tanker market, the freight futures market and the oil price have turned (#1); the long-standing owner sold out at about USD 40 a month ago; owners across the industry are ordering ships; and the only estimate line with more room to fall than to rise is the outer year.

Inference. The dashboard's rule reads trailing momentum and the multiple, and both lag in a business whose earnings reprice with every voyage. On the forward drivers the stock is in late Reinforcing, with Stalling beginning. My expected sequence is: Reinforcing in the reported numbers until 3 March 2027; Stalling through the first half of 2027, as quarterly dividends step down and investors question FY2028; decline through late 2027 and 2028 in the base case; and Bottoming in 2028 to 2029, when deliveries meet a resumption of scrapping.

So what. The phases that match Richard's setups, Bottoming and Turning up, lie beyond the 12 to 24 month window in the base case and inside it only in the early-normalisation case. If I am right about the phase, the peak-phase multiple that the dashboard's rule assigns is the wrong multiple (#11).

Counter-case. Persistence (20% likely) would hold the stock in Reinforcing through 2027, with further estimate upgrades and about USD 3 a share of extra dividend.
What would change my view. Product tanker rates and LR2 counts holding through January, and a March guidance range above consensus, would argue that Broadening is the right label for another two or three quarters.
Against the market. The sell-side behaves as though the thesis is still broadening. The share price behaves as though the thesis is stalling. I side with the share price.
Score: 28set by the Rater. The computed Broadening misreads a windfall: on the forward drivers the stock is at peak delivery, in late Reinforcing with Stalling beginning (shares falling on good news, crude rates, futures and oil turned, the long-time owner sold out, industry ordering ships), and the next six to twelve months bring stepping-down dividends and the first decline in estimates. Four months of reported good news to March keep it a little above Maersk's level, just below Zegona.
#11

The fair multiple

The guideline multiple of 8.86 times is a fair, slightly conservative anchor, because a late-cycle phase argues for less and a debt-free balance sheet for more, and no multiple inside TORM's normal range produces a positive return on the model's earnings.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple is 8.86 times two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of TORM's own ten-year history (113 of 120 months, outliers removed), set for the Broadening phase that the dashboard assigns. The ten-year range is 3.1 times at the 10th percentile, 5.8 at the median, 8.2 at the 75th and 11.0 at the 90th. The shares trade at 9.3 times consensus earnings and at 13.1 times the model's.

My view of the guideline multiple, in three steps.

1 · LOWER
Judged by the lifecycle phase, 8.86 times is generous. Viewforth's framework puts higher multiples on peak delivery and lower ones on Stalling. I think the stock is later than Broadening (#10), and at the last peak the market paid 6.6 times and took the multiple to 3.8 times within six months.
→
2 · HIGHER
Judged by what the earnings will be at the horizon, 8.86 times is somewhat low. By March 2028 the two-year-forward EPS (about USD 1.64) is mid-cycle earnings on a nearly debt-free balance sheet. At 8.86 times the shares would be about USD 14.5: about 0.55 times book value, about 0.4 times the NAV estimated in the second set of research and about 3.4 times EBITDA. In 2025, at a similar fleet rate but with USD 0.7bn to 0.8bn of net debt, the market paid about 4 to 5 times EBITDA (my calculation from that year's share price range and net debt). Putting 4.0 to 4.5 times on EBITDA of about USD 500m and deducting about USD 0.1bn to 0.2bn of net debt gives USD 17 to 21 a share, which is 10.5 to 13 times the same EPS. The windfall has moved value from lenders to shareholders, and a price-to-earnings multiple struck in geared years does not capture that shift.
→
3 · IT DOES NOT MATTER
The two points pull in opposite directions, and the conclusion does not depend on which one wins. For the return to 31 March 2028 to reach zero, the multiple would have to be about 16 times the model's earnings, above the 90th percentile of TORM's ten-year range.

So what. I accept 8.86 times as a reasonable central anchor, mildly conservative for a de-geared TORM, with 8 to 13 times as my plausible band at the horizon. The live disagreement with the market is about earnings, not the multiple: on consensus earnings the shares already sit at the guideline.

Counter-case. Tanker shares have found their floor on assets. If ship values fall only 20% to 25% and the shares trough at 0.6 to 0.7 times NAV, the price is USD 20 to 26, which is 12 to 16 times mid-cycle EPS. That outcome needs ship values to hold up while the equity earns only about 6% on that NAV, about half the return of 2025 (my calculation); one of the two would have to give.
What would change my view. Secondhand ship values holding in a normalised market would move me toward the top of my band; a de-rating of the tanker group on unchanged estimates, as happened in late 2024, would move me toward the bottom.
Against the market. The market's multiple (9.3 times consensus) and the guideline (8.86) agree. The brokers' targets sit above today's NAV (a mean of about USD 46 against 39.60). I think both the earnings and the NAV behind those targets are peak figures.
Score: 29set by the Rater. Dear on one and neutral on the other gives D; I place it low in the band because the dear reading flatters (on the model's earnings the multiple is 13.1x, above the 90th percentile) and a stock entering Stalling deserves less than its history, only partly offset by a de-gearing balance sheet that argues for a somewhat higher multiple at the horizon.

What each part of the return to March 2028 means.

  • Dividends (+26.8%) are about USD 9.6 a share: the Q4 2026 dividend and the four dividends declared for FY2027. The dividends are the solid part of the return, and about 38% of them is declared on one date, 3 March 2027. A holder on the register on 17 November 2026 also receives the Q3 dividend of USD 1.35.
  • Earnings (-40.4%) is the two-year-forward EPS rolling from about USD 2.7, a window that still catches the end of the disruption, to about 1.64, a window entirely at the settled rate.
  • The multiple (-32.1%) is 13.1 times falling to 8.86. The fall in the multiple is better read as the model's disagreement with consensus about the settled rate: on consensus earnings the shares already trade at 8.7 to 9.3 times.

The shape through time. The cash comes first and the capital loss later. Over the next six months the return is dominated by one near-certain dividend worth 10% of the price and by how the tanker group trades around the turn, which no model column captures. Between March 2028 and September 2029 almost nothing changes: the multiple is constant, earnings are flat at the floor, and the extra 4.4 points of return are a year and a half of small dividends. On the model, the shares after the fade are dead money at a low price.

What drives the return, in order of importance.

  1. The settled rate (Judgement 2). The return to March 2028 is zero if the fleet rate settles near USD 30,000 per day instead of about 26,000, and about +20% at USD 33,000, which lies between the two named brokers' rates.
  2. The valuation anchor the market uses. On my enterprise-value cross-check (USD 17 to 21 a share) the return to March 2028 is about -26% to -15%; on a trough multiple of NAV (USD 20 to 26) it is about -18% to -1%.
  3. The timing of the fade (Judgement 1). Each quarter of timing is worth about USD 2.0 of dividend, 5.5% of the price. Time alone does not rescue the return: in the persistence case I estimate roughly -10% to +10%, because by March 2028 the fade would still lie ahead. In the early-normalisation case I estimate about -40% at the guideline multiple. Weighted across the four scenarios, the return is about -30% at the guideline multiple.

#13

Summary conclusion

TORM is the best commercial operator in a business that gives its owners no control over price. In 2026 that business is earning the largest windfall in its history from closed straits, rerouted ships and a migration of large tankers into crude, and TORM is converting the windfall with discipline into dividends and a debt-free balance sheet. Those strengths are real and worth having.

The investment case over 12 to 24 months runs the other way. The forces behind the windfall are reversible, linked and already weakening at the leading edge, and TORM has no internal driver to replace them. Guidance and estimates have about four months of favourable news left, after which the estimate most likely to be cut is FY2028, the year the valuation rests on. Momentum is at its maximum, the lifecycle is at its peak, and the model's return is about -33%, softened but not reversed by any asset-based cross-check.

What Richard looks for, fundamental outcomes and upgrade probabilities unusually skewed to the positive, is not present in TORM today: the skew is negative in size and in speed. Three things would change that, and none is in TORM's hands: disruption that persists, a settled rate near USD 30,000 per day, or an offer from Hafnia on fair terms.

The practical value of this work is that the case can be watched cheaply and precisely. One variable, published weekly, with stated thresholds (#9), tells the reader which path the stock is on, and one date, 3 March 2027, will reveal management's own view of 2027 in figures.

On the far side of the fade, a debt-free TORM with its rate premium intact, at a trough multiple of trough earnings, would be a different and much better-fitting case. Four signposts would mark that case:

The four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength15
15, set by the Rater. The input forces are net strongly negative over the case's horizon, a reversing scarcity windfall plus a dated supply wave (topic 1 at 20) with no internal self-help to offset it (topic 2 at 48), and that change reaches profits surely and sharply, EPS falling about 81% from FY2026 to FY2028 and ending below FY2025 (topic 6 F); a smaller order book and near-locked near-term quarters keep it just above Maersk.
Foundations' Robustness33
33, set by the Rater. A top-tier, transparent operator with clean earnings and a balance sheet becoming debt-free sits inside a fragmented, price-taking industry with no moat beyond a 10% rate premium, higher breakeven than peers, low single-digit returns in past troughs and ordinary capital allocation (topic 3 at 32), while the delivery record shows guidance that is reliable only for the current year and cut when rates fade (topic 4 at 57), so it sits near Maersk in the 25 to 50 range, a little above.
Setups' Fit/Crispness9
9, set by the Rater. In substance the case is the inverse of a Target Setup: a temporary windfall at peak earnings, not a step-up in earnings power or a trough, and the memo's nearest fit (CfC in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough) needs the fade to have happened, so today's peak position contradicts its mechanism; like Maersk's windfall case at the point a setup would sell.
Case Riskiness20
20, set by the Rater. The case is simple, single-factor, well disclosed and solvent in every scenario, but that one factor is unforecastable, moves in weeks, gives a -60% to +65% cone on next year's EPS and a fair trough 40% to 50% below the price (topic 9 at 19); weekly trackability and low debt lift it slightly above Maersk's similar single-price case.

End notes

Prices and sources: the share price is DKK 238.6 (about USD 35.7) on 11 November 2026; the model and the total return calculation use DKK 239.8 (about USD 35.9). The forecasts are those of the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Probabilities, scenario weights and cross-checks are my own estimates unless a source is named; "the second set of research" refers to the second set of research files supplied for this memo, which is the source of the scenarios in #9, the post-fall NAV of USD 34 to 38 and the Hafnia overhead saving.

Three differences of basis in the model (#6): first, the model's revenue is 30% to 40% "above consensus" only because consensus revenue is TCE; on TCE the gaps are 0%, +3% and -8% for FY2026 to FY2028. Second, the model books each fourth-quarter dividend in the year it relates to, so net debt at the end of 2026 is really about USD 420m to 450m, not 733m. Third, the model's 2028 quarters fall through the year where the intention was a level path; the full-year figure is right.

Checks and limits: the latest Earnings Review in the research covers the Q3 2026 results published on 4 November 2026, the last reported period. The research holds no notes from the four brokers that publish estimates on TORM, so their narrative is inferred from their numbers, and it holds no direct investor commentary, so investors' views are inferred from prices and positioning.

Visuals: history is FactSet's reported basis; consensus is FactSet's (median unless stated, on the brokers' basis, where "revenue" is TCE); forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Charts drawn for this memo (EPS against the fleet rate, the fleet rate against its history and other views, the dividend staircase, the scenario range and the return under each view) take their figures from the memo text. Share prices and targets are in DKK where stated, otherwise USD.

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

  • Consensus net income for FY2026 is 1,157.75, +296.5% against 292.00 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +37.0%.
  • Consensus earnings per share for FY2026 is 11.23, +289.9% against 2.88 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +37.0%.
